demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette: Samir had spent forty-two years on American university campuses as an environmental scientist, but his career shifted into narrow, guarded passages eighteen months ago at a state-run hydrology monitoring station. He had been calibrating a pressure gauge when a fractured seal released a wave of superheated steam and collapsed steel framework. His colleague, a junior field technician, was pinned against the bulkhead. Samir remembered the violent shearing of metal, then the terrible, ragged inhalation as the man fought against the weight until emergency responders cut through the door. The technical review cleared him of negligence, citing a hidden manufacturing flaw, but the official documentation could not reach the quiet, physical certainty that had taken root in Samir’s chest. He knew what he had done. He had been the one standing beside the man when the framework gave way. In the weeks that followed, the memory refused to stay filed away. When Samir closed his eyes, he did not recall the incident; he was back in the cold concrete room, the smell of scorched rubber filling his throat, his palms pressed against the same unyielding steel. The sensation was so immediate that he would wake with his breath caught, certain he had not left the site. Over time, the enormity of the event grew distant and difficult to reconcile with his own history. He would sit in his study at the department, staring at the incident report, thinking that the man trapped beneath the weight could not possibly be someone he knew. It felt like a story written about another person, one that should have happened elsewhere, to someone else. Yet the truth remained lodged in his ribs: he had been there. He simply could not find the words to explain it to anyone. When his wife, Nora, asked what had happened, his throat would close, the syllables dissolving before they could leave his mouth. His work environment became a landscape of careful navigation. He avoided the east wing laboratory where the ventilation system cycled with audible, forceful exhalations. One Tuesday, a graduate student burst into his office, late with sediment samples, his chest rising and falling in a deep, uneven rhythm as he apologized for running up four flights of stairs. Samir felt his shoulders lock. The sound of that heavy breathing filled the room like a physical presence. He stood abruptly, claiming he needed to verify a calibration log, and walked to the archives, where the air was still and quiet. He told himself he was simply managing his schedule, but the retreat was automatic, born of the need to escape the sound that matched his own desperate gasps at the moment the framework collapsed. At home, the avoidance took different forms. He had come to distrust the quiet moments when he finally let his guard down. A weekend morning spent watching the birds from the porch, a book resting on his lap, would suddenly feel untenable. His shoulders would rise, his jaw would clench, and he would get up to tackle the sink, just to keep his hands moving. When Nora reached for him in bed, her hand resting against his shoulder or offering a slow, deliberate hug, Samir’s body would stiffen. He did not pull away harshly, but the tension in his neck and the rigid set of his back made the embrace shallow and distant. He loved her, but the physical contact carried a weight he could not navigate. These habits accumulated over a year and a half. He declined invitations to departmental dinners, canceled hiking trips with colleagues, and learned to sit on the far side of the sofa. His marriage grew careful; Nora stopped reaching for him, and the space between them widened not from anger, but from a quiet, mutual hesitation. What finally brought him to seek help was a still Tuesday evening. He had been sitting at his desk, reviewing a state grant proposal, when he realized he had not spoken a full sentence aloud in three days. He looked at the stack of unopened mail, the untouched garden gloves by the door, and the way Nora moved around him like a guest in her own home. He knew he needed to name what he was carrying, even if his mouth had long ago forgotten how. He hoped, more than anything, to find a way to sit in the same room as his own life without bracing for the next collapse.
